claim: Key enzymatic processes use the nonequilibrium error correction mechanism called kinetic proofreading to enhance their specificity.
source: Key enzymatic processes use the nonequilibrium error correction mechanism called kinetic proofreading to enhance their specificity.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinetic proofreading that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Traditional proofreading schemes typically require dedicated structural features in the enzyme, such as a nucleotide hydrolysis site or multiple intermediate conformations.
source: The applicability of traditional proofreading schemes, however, is limited because they typically require dedicated structural features in the enzyme, such as a nucleotide hydrolysis site or multiple intermediate conformations.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established knowledge about traditional proofreading mechanisms and is elaborated with specific examples in the introduction.

claim: Spatial proofreading achieves error correction by having substrate binding and subsequent product formation occur at distinct physical locations.
source: Here, we explore an alternative conceptual mechanism that achieves error correction by having substrate binding and subsequent product formation occur at distinct physical locations.
evidence: This is the central theoretical proposal of the manuscript, supported by the mathematical modeling and analysis presented throughout.

claim: The time taken by the enzyme–substrate complex to diffuse from one location to another is leveraged to discard wrong substrates in spatial proofreading.
source: The time taken by the enzyme–substrate complex to diffuse from one location to another is leveraged to discard wrong substrates.
evidence: This is a theoretical mechanism proposed and analyzed through mathematical modeling in the manuscript.

claim: Spatial proofreading does not have the typical structural requirements of traditional proofreading mechanisms.
source: This mechanism does not have the typical structural requirements, making it easier to overlook in experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical model which does not require dedicated enzyme features like hydrolysis sites.

claim: Kinetic proofreading was described by Hopfield in 1974 and Ninio in 1975.
source: The nonequilibrium mechanism called kinetic proofreading (Hopfield, 1974; Ninio, 1975) is used for reducing the error rates of many biochemical processes important for cell function
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original papers by Hopfield and Ninio.

claim: Kinetic proofreading is used in DNA replication.
source: (e.g. DNA replication [Kunkel, 2004], transcription [Sydow and Cramer, 2009], translation [Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Ieong et al., 2016], signal transduction [Swain and Siggia, 2002], or pathogen recognition [McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; Cui and Mehta, 2018])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kunkel, 2004.

claim: Kinetic proofreading is used in transcription.
source: (e.g. DNA replication [Kunkel, 2004], transcription [Sydow and Cramer, 2009], translation [Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Ieong et al., 2016], signal transduction [Swain and Siggia, 2002], or pathogen recognition [McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; Cui and Mehta, 2018])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sydow and Cramer, 2009.

claim: Kinetic proofreading is used in translation.
source: (e.g. DNA replication [Kunkel, 2004], transcription [Sydow and Cramer, 2009], translation [Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Ieong et al., 2016], signal transduction [Swain and Siggia, 2002], or pathogen recognition [McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; Cui and Mehta, 2018])
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001 and Ieong et al., 2016.

claim: Kinetic proofreading is used in signal transduction.
source: (e.g. DNA replication [Kunkel, 2004], transcription [Sydow and Cramer, 2009], translation [Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Ieong et al., 2016], signal transduction [Swain and Siggia, 2002], or pathogen recognition [McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; Cui and Mehta, 2018])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swain and Siggia, 2002.

claim: Kinetic proofreading is used in pathogen recognition.
source: (e.g. DNA replication [Kunkel, 2004], transcription [Sydow and Cramer, 2009], translation [Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001; Ieong et al., 2016], signal transduction [Swain and Siggia, 2002], or pathogen recognition [McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; Cui and Mehta, 2018])
evidence: This is supported by citations to McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004; and Cui and Mehta, 2018.

claim: Proofreading mechanisms operate by inducing a delay between substrate binding and product formation via intermediate states for the enzyme–substrate complex.
source: Proofreading mechanisms operate by inducing a delay between substrate binding and product formation via intermediate states for the enzyme–substrate complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how proofreading mechanisms work.

claim: The delay in proofreading gives the enzyme multiple chances to release the wrong substrate after initial binding.
source: Such a delay gives the enzyme multiple chances to release the wrong substrate after initial binding, allowing far lower error rates than what one would expect solely from the binding energy difference between right and wrong substrates.
evidence: This is an established principle of kinetic proofreading mechanisms.

claim: DNA polymerases have an exonuclease pocket as a dedicated molecular feature for proofreading.
source: Traditional proofreading schemes require dedicated molecular features such as an exonuclease pocket in DNA polymerases (Kunkel, 2004) or multiple phosphorylation sites on T-cell receptors (McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kunkel, 2004.

claim: T-cell receptors have multiple phosphorylation sites as dedicated molecular features for proofreading.
source: Traditional proofreading schemes require dedicated molecular features such as an exonuclease pocket in DNA polymerases (Kunkel, 2004) or multiple phosphorylation sites on T-cell receptors (McKeithan, 1995; Goldstein et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to McKeithan, 1995 and Goldstein et al., 2004.

claim: Proofreading is an active nonequilibrium process often involving near-irreversible reactions.
source: Additionally, since proofreading is an active nonequilibrium process often involving near–irreversible reactions, the enzyme typically needs to have an ATP or GTP hydrolysis site to enable the use of energy supplies of the cell (Yamane and Hopfield, 1977; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamane and Hopfield, 1977 and Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001.

claim: Proofreading enzymes typically need an ATP or GTP hydrolysis site to enable the use of energy supplies of the cell.
source: Additionally, since proofreading is an active nonequilibrium process often involving near–irreversible reactions, the enzyme typically needs to have an ATP or GTP hydrolysis site to enable the use of energy supplies of the cell (Yamane and Hopfield, 1977; Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamane and Hopfield, 1977 and Rodnina and Wintermeyer, 2001.

claim: The number of confirmed proofreading enzymes is relatively small due to stringent structural requirements.
source: Due to such stringent structural requirements, the number of confirmed proofreading enzymes is relatively small.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of structural requirements and the state of the field.

claim: Generic enzymes without dedicated proofreading features are assumed to not have active error correction available to them.
source: Furthermore, generic enzymes without such dedicated features are assumed to not have active error correction available to them.
evidence: This represents the conventional understanding in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: In spatial proofreading, the delay between binding and catalysis is created by constraining these events to distinct physical locations.
source: In this work, we propose an alternative scheme where the delay between initial substrate binding and product formation steps is achieved by separating these events in space.
evidence: This is the core theoretical proposal of the manuscript.

claim: Wrong substrates are assumed to unbind from the enzyme more readily than the right substrates in spatial proofreading.
source: If substrates are spatially localized and product formation is favorable only in a region of low substrate concentration where an activating effector is present then the time taken by the enzyme–substrate complex to travel from one location to the other can be used to discard the wrong substrates, which are assumed to unbind from the enzyme more readily than the right substrates (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an assumption built into the theoretical model.

claim: When the delay is longer than substrate unbinding time scales, very low error rates of product formation can be achieved in spatial proofreading.
source: When this delay is longer than substrate unbinding time scales, very low error rates of product formation can be achieved, allowing this spatial proofreading scheme to outperform biochemical mechanisms with a finite number of proofreading steps.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model analysis.

claim: Spatial proofreading can outperform biochemical mechanisms with a finite number of proofreading steps.
source: When this delay is longer than substrate unbinding time scales, very low error rates of product formation can be achieved, allowing this spatial proofreading scheme to outperform biochemical mechanisms with a finite number of proofreading steps.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model analysis comparing spatial proofreading to traditional schemes.

claim: Spatial proofreading does not require any direct energy consumption by the enzyme or substrate itself through ATP hydrolysis.
source: In contrast to traditional proofreading, the nonequilibrium mechanism here does not require any direct energy consumption by the enzyme or substrate itself (e.g. through ATP hydrolysis).
evidence: This is a feature of the proposed theoretical mechanism.

claim: Any equilibrium enzyme with a localized effector can proofread using spatial proofreading if appropriate concentration gradients of the substrates or enzymes are set up.
source: This liberates the enzyme from any proofreading-specific molecular features; indeed, any 'equilibrium' enzyme with a localized effector can proofread using our scheme if appropriate concentration gradients of the substrates or enzymes are set up.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The energetic and structural requirements of proofreading can be outsourced from the enzyme and substrate to the gradient maintaining mechanism in spatial proofreading.
source: In this way, the energetic and structural requirements of proofreading can be outsourced from the enzyme and substrate to the gradient maintaining mechanism.
evidence: This is a conceptual implication of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Spatial proofreading is easy to overlook in experiments.
source: It also means that spatial proofreading is easy to overlook in experiments, and that the fidelity of reconstituted reactions in vitro could be lower than the fidelity in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that the mechanism does not require dedicated structural features.

claim: The fidelity of reconstituted reactions in vitro could be lower than the fidelity in vivo for spatial proofreading.
source: It also means that spatial proofreading is easy to overlook in experiments, and that the fidelity of reconstituted reactions in vitro could be lower than the fidelity in vivo.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the dependence of spatial proofreading on cellular gradients that may not be present in vitro.

claim: The lack of reliance on structure makes spatial proofreading more adaptable.
source: The lack of reliance on structure makes spatial proofreading more adaptable.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with traditional proofreading mechanisms.

claim: Tuning the length scale of concentration gradients can trade off error rate against speed and energy consumption in spatial proofreading.
source: We study how tuning the length scale of concentration gradients can trade off error rate against speed and energy consumption on the fly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the mathematical analysis and figures in the manuscript.

claim: Traditional proofreading schemes rely on nucleotide chemical potentials and cannot modulate their operation without broader physiological disruptions.
source: In contrast, traditional proofreading schemes rely on nucleotide chemical potentials, for example, the out of equilibrium [ATP]/[ADP] ratio in the cell, and cannot modulate their operation without broader physiological disruptions.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about how traditional proofreading mechanisms operate.

claim: Concentration gradients arise near the nucleus, the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the endoplasmic reticulum, kinetochores, and microtubules.
source: Such gradients arise in multiple cellular contexts (e.g. near the nucleus, the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the endoplasmic reticulum [ER], kinetochores, microtubules [Bivona et al., 2003; Caudron et al., 2005; Kholodenko, 2006])
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bivona et al., 2003; Caudron et al., 2005; and Kholodenko, 2006.

claim: Several gradient-forming mechanisms have been discussed in the literature.
source: and several gradient-forming mechanisms have been discussed in the literature (Wu et al., 2018; Kholodenko, 2006; Kholodenko, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2018; Kholodenko, 2006; and Kholodenko, 2003.

claim: The model extends to scenarios where the two substrates have different localization length scales.
source: In Appendix 4, we extend our study of model performance to the scenario where the two substrates have different localization length scales.
evidence: This is stated as an extension of the model presented in the appendix.

claim: The assumption that enzymes are mostly free makes the model equations linear and allows analytical solution at steady state.
source: This assumption makes Equations (1-3) linear and allows us to solve them analytically at steady state.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the modeling assumption.

claim: Proofreading is most effective under the assumption of low substrate amounts.
source: We demonstrate in Appendix 5 that proofreading is, in fact, most effective under this assumption and discuss the consequences of having high substrate amounts on the performance of the scheme.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis presented in Appendix 5.

claim: Enzyme activation and catalysis take place upon reaching the right boundary at a rate r that is identical for both substrates.
source: In our simplified picture, enzyme activation and catalysis take place upon reaching the right boundary at a rate r that is identical for both substrates.
evidence: This is an assumption of the simplified model.

claim: The main analyses are performed under the assumption that catalysis is slow.
source: In order to keep the analytical results concise and intuitive, we perform our main analyses under the assumption that catalysis is slow, mirroring the study of traditional proofreading schemes (Hopfield, 1974).
evidence: This is an explicit modeling choice, with citation to Hopfield, 1974 for comparison.

claim: The fidelity enhancement in spatial proofreading comes at a cost of reduced product formation speed.
source: As is inherent to all proofreading schemes, the fidelity enhancement described earlier comes at a cost of reduced product formation speed.
evidence: This is a general principle of proofreading mechanisms and is demonstrated in the model.

claim: The reduction in speed happens because of increased delays in diffusive transport.
source: This reduction, in our case, happens because of increased delays in diffusive transport.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of spatial proofreading.

claim: With tighter substrate localization, the complexes are formed closer to the left boundary, and a smaller fraction of complexes reach the activation region, reducing reaction speed.
source: This trade-off is intuitive; with tighter substrate localization, the complexes are formed closer to the left boundary. Hence, a smaller fraction of complexes reach the activation region, reducing reaction speed.
evidence: This is a logical explanation of the observed trade-off.

claim: In the limit of slow diffusion, both types of complexes have exponentially low densities at the activation region, but production is highly accurate.
source: In the opposite limit of slow diffusion, both types of complexes have exponentially low densities at the activation region, but due to the difference in substrate off-rates, production is highly accurate (Figure 3b, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3b and explained in the text.

claim: There exists an intermediate regime where a significant fraction of right complexes reach the activation region while the vast majority of wrong complexes do not.
source: There also exists an intermediate regime where a significant fraction of right complexes reach the activation region while the vast majority of wrong complexes do not (Figure 3b, middle).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3b.

claim: In the intermediate regime, a moderate decrease in the production rate yields high fidelity enhancement.
source: As a result, an advantageous trade-off is achieved where a moderate decrease in the production rate yields high fidelity enhancement – a feature that was also identified in multi-step traditional proofreading models (Murugan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model and compared to traditional proofreading with citation to Murugan et al., 2012.

claim: Proofreading is a nonequilibrium mechanism with an associated free energy cost.
source: A hallmark signature of proofreading is that it is a nonequilibrium mechanism with an associated free energy cost.
evidence: This is established knowledge about proofreading mechanisms.

claim: In spatial proofreading, the enzyme itself is not directly involved in any energy-consuming reactions, such as hydrolysis.
source: In our scheme, the enzyme itself is not directly involved in any energy-consuming reactions, such as hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a feature of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The free energy cost in spatial proofreading comes from maintaining the spatial gradient of substrates.
source: Instead, the free energy cost comes from maintaining the spatial gradient of substrates, which the enzymatic reaction tends to homogenize by releasing bound substrates in regions of low substrate concentration.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermodynamic analysis of the mechanism.

claim: There exists a thermodynamically dictated minimum energy that any gradient maintenance mechanism must dissipate per unit time.
source: While mechanisms of substrate gradient maintenance may differ in their energetic efficiency, there exists a thermodynamically dictated minimum energy that any such mechanism must dissipate per unit time.
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: For the bulk of each curve, power scales as the logarithm of fidelity.
source: For the bulk of each curve, power scales as the logarithm of fidelity, suggesting that a linear increase in dissipation can yield an exponential reduction in error.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4.

claim: A linear increase in dissipation can yield an exponential reduction in error.
source: For the bulk of each curve, power scales as the logarithm of fidelity, suggesting that a linear increase in dissipation can yield an exponential reduction in error.
evidence: This is inferred from the logarithmic scaling relationship.

claim: A logarithmic scaling relationship between dissipation and adaptation error has been calculated in the context of E. coli chemoreceptor adaptation.
source: Notably, such a scaling relationship has also been calculated in the context of E. coli chemoreceptor adaptation (Lan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lan et al., 2012.

claim: In E. coli chemoreceptor adaptation, the adaptation error decreases exponentially with energy dissipated through multiple methylation-demethylation cycles.
source: In particular, it was shown that the adaptation error decreases exponentially with energy dissipated through multiple methylation–demethylation cycles which are used to stabilize the activity state of the receptor.
evidence: This is based on the cited work on chemoreceptor adaptation.

claim: Beyond the optimal driving force range, additional error correction is attained at an increasingly higher cost.
source: And beyond the range, additional error correction is attained at an increasingly higher cost.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4 where the curves diverge.

claim: The power computed does not include the baseline cost of creating the substrate gradient.
source: Note that the power computed here does not include the baseline cost of creating the substrate gradient, which, for instance, would depend on the substrate diffusion constant.
evidence: This is an explicit clarification about what is included in the power calculation.

claim: The calculated power only accounts for the additional cost due to the operation of the proofreading scheme which works to homogenize the substrate gradient.
source: We only account for the additional cost to be paid due to the operation of the proofreading scheme which works to homogenize this substrate gradient.
evidence: This is an explicit clarification about what is included in the power calculation.

claim: The scaling behavior (η/ηeq)max ≈ exp(βΔμ)/(βΔμ) was theoretically accessible only to infinite-state traditional proofreading schemes.
source: Such scaling behavior was theoretically accessible only to infinite-state traditional proofreading schemes (Qian, 2006; Ehrenberg and Blomberg, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qian, 2006 and Ehrenberg and Blomberg, 1980.

claim: Spatial proofreading can be viewed as a procession of the enzyme through an infinite series of spatial filters.
source: This offers a view of spatial proofreading as a procession of the enzyme through an infinite series of spatial filters
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism based on its performance characteristics.

claim: From the perspective of peak error reduction capacity, spatial proofreading outperforms finite-state traditional proofreading schemes.
source: and suggests that, from the perspective of peak error reduction capacity, our model outperforms the finite-state schemes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of scaling behaviors.

claim: The model investigates proofreading based on a mechanism for creating gradients by the spatial separation of two opposing enzymes.
source: Here, we investigate proofreading based on a widely applicable mechanism for creating gradients by the spatial separation of two opposing enzymes (Stelling and Kholodenko, 2009; Bivona et al., 2003; Brown and Kholodenko, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stelling and Kholodenko, 2009; Bivona et al., 2003; and Brown and Kholodenko, 1999.

claim: Kinase/phosphatase mechanisms create gradients of the active forms of MEK and ERK.
source: Such mechanisms are known to create gradients of the active forms of MEK and ERK (Kholodenko, 2006), of GTPases such as Ran (with GEF and GAP [Kalab et al., 2002] playing the role of kinase and phosphatase, respectively), of cAMP (Kholodenko, 2006) and of stathmin oncoprotein 18 (Op18) (Bastiaens et al., 2006; Niethammer et al., 2004) near the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the ER, kinetochores and other places.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kholodenko, 2006.

claim: Kinase/phosphatase mechanisms create gradients of GTPases such as Ran.
source: Such mechanisms are known to create gradients of the active forms of MEK and ERK (Kholodenko, 2006), of GTPases such as Ran (with GEF and GAP [Kalab et al., 2002] playing the role of kinase and phosphatase, respectively), of cAMP (Kholodenko, 2006) and of stathmin oncoprotein 18 (Op18) (Bastiaens et al., 2006; Niethammer et al., 2004) near the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the ER, kinetochores and other places.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalab et al., 2002.

claim: Kinase/phosphatase mechanisms create gradients of cAMP.
source: Such mechanisms are known to create gradients of the active forms of MEK and ERK (Kholodenko, 2006), of GTPases such as Ran (with GEF and GAP [Kalab et al., 2002] playing the role of kinase and phosphatase, respectively), of cAMP (Kholodenko, 2006) and of stathmin oncoprotein 18 (Op18) (Bastiaens et al., 2006; Niethammer et al., 2004) near the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the ER, kinetochores and other places.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kholodenko, 2006.

claim: Kinase/phosphatase mechanisms create gradients of stathmin oncoprotein 18 (Op18).
source: Such mechanisms are known to create gradients of the active forms of MEK and ERK (Kholodenko, 2006), of GTPases such as Ran (with GEF and GAP [Kalab et al., 2002] playing the role of kinase and phosphatase, respectively), of cAMP (Kholodenko, 2006) and of stathmin oncoprotein 18 (Op18) (Bastiaens et al., 2006; Niethammer et al., 2004) near the plasma membrane, the Golgi apparatus, the ER, kinetochores and other places.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bastiaens et al., 2006 and Niethammer et al., 2004.

claim: The off-rates 0.1 s-1 and 1 s-1 are consistent with typical values for substrates proofread by cellular signaling systems.
source: These off-rates are consistent with typical values for substrates proofread by cellular signaling systems (Cui and Mehta, 2018; Gascoigne et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cui and Mehta, 2018 and Gascoigne et al., 2001.

claim: The kinases and phosphatases in the model act identically on right and wrong substrates.
source: The kinases and phosphatases in our setup act identically on right and wrong substrates.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The kinase/phosphatase setup achieves proofreading in a wide range of regimes, though not cost-efficiently.
source: Although not cost-efficient, this setup achieves proofreading in a wide range of regimes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the analysis of the biochemically detailed model.

claim: The kinase/phosphatase setup is most effective when the enzyme-substrate binding is slow, in which case the exponential substrate profile is maintained.
source: Specifically, it is most effective when the enzyme–substrate binding is slow, in which case the exponential substrate profile is maintained and the system attains the fidelity predicted by our earlier explanatory model (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b.

claim: Enzymes can work at reasonable binding rates and still proofread when accounting for an experimentally characterized gradient maintaining mechanism.
source: Overall, this model suggests that enzymes can work at reasonable binding rates and still proofread, when accounting for an experimentally characterized gradient maintaining mechanism.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the analysis of the biochemically detailed model.

claim: Spatial proofreading is based on a time delay due to spatial transport rather than transitions through biochemical intermediates.
source: Like the classic model, our proposed spatial proofreading scheme is based on a time delay; but unlike the classic model, here the delay is due to spatial transport rather than transitions through biochemical intermediates.
evidence: This is the key conceptual distinction of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Spatial proofreading exploits the free energy supplied by active mechanisms that maintain spatial structures.
source: Instead, our scheme exploits the free energy supplied by active mechanisms that maintain spatial structures.
evidence: This is a feature of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The decoupling of time delay and free energy dissipation allows the cell to tune proofreading on the fly.
source: The decoupling of the two crucial features of proofreading – time delay and free energy dissipation – allows the cell to tune proofreading on the fly.
evidence: This is inferred from the modular nature of the mechanism.

claim: For traditional proofreading schemes, navigating the speed-fidelity trade-off is not always feasible as it needs to involve structural changes via mutations or modulation of the [ATP]/[ADP] ratio which can cause collateral effects.
source: For traditional schemes, navigating this trade-off is not always feasible, as it needs to involve structural changes via mutations or modulation of the [ATP]/[ADP] ratio which can cause collateral effects on the rest of the cell.
evidence: This is based on understanding of how traditional proofreading mechanisms operate.

claim: Spatial proofreading is more adaptable to the changing conditions and needs of the cell.
source: In contrast, the spatial proofreading scheme is more adaptable to the changing conditions and needs of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the tunability of the mechanism.

claim: The spatial proofreading scheme can prioritize speed in one context and fidelity in another by tuning the length scale of intracellular gradients.
source: The scheme can prioritize speed in one context, and fidelity in another, simply by tuning the length scale of intracellular gradients (e.g. through the regulation of the phosphotase or free enzyme concentration in the scheme discussed earlier).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the model's tunability.

claim: The modular decoupling in spatial proofreading can complicate the experimental identification of proofreading enzymes.
source: On the other hand, this modular decoupling can complicate the experimental identification of proofreading enzymes and the interpretation of their fidelity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of dedicated structural features.

claim: Enzymes using spatial proofreading need not be endowed with the structural and biochemical properties typically sought for in a proofreading enzyme.
source: Here, the enzymes need not be endowed with the structural and biochemical properties typically sought for in a proofreading enzyme.
evidence: This is a consequence of the mechanism not requiring dedicated structural features.

claim: Any attempt to reconstitute enzymatic activity using spatial proofreading in a well-mixed, in vitro assay will show poor fidelity compared to in vivo measurements, even when all necessary molecular players are present in vitro.
source: At the same time, any attempt to reconstitute enzymatic activity in a well-mixed, in vitro assay, will show poor fidelity compared to in vivo measurements, even when all necessary molecular players are present in vitro.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the dependence of the mechanism on spatial gradients.

claim: The framework applies equally well to scenarios with a spatially localized enzyme (or its active form) and effector with delocalized substrates.
source: While we focused on spatially localized substrates and delocalized enzymes, our framework would apply equally well to other scenarios, like one with a spatially localized enzyme (or its active form [Kalab et al., 2002; Nalbant et al., 2004]) and effector with delocalized substrates
evidence: This is stated as a generalization of the framework with supporting citations.

claim: The framework can be extended to signaling cascades where slightly different phosphatase activities can result in magnified concentration ratios of two competing signaling molecules.
source: Our framework can also be extended to signaling cascades, where slightly different phosphatase activities can result in magnified concentration ratios of two competing signaling molecules at the spatial location of the next cascade step (Roy and Cyert, 2009; Bauman and Scott, 2002; Kholodenko, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as an extension with supporting citations to Roy and Cyert, 2009; Bauman and Scott, 2002; and Kholodenko, 2006.

claim: Spatial gradients needed for the model can be created through passive diffusion of substrates/ligands combined with active degradation.
source: The spatial gradients needed for the operation of our model can be created and maintained through multiple mechanisms in the cell, ranging from the kinase/phosphatase system modeled here, to the passive diffusion of substrates/ligands combined with active degradation (e.g. Bicoid and other developmental morphogens), to active transport processes combined with diffusion.
evidence: This is stated as one of several possible gradient formation mechanisms.

claim: Bicoid and other developmental morphogens form gradients through passive diffusion combined with active degradation.
source: to the passive diffusion of substrates/ligands combined with active degradation (e.g. Bicoid and other developmental morphogens)
evidence: This is cited as an example of gradient formation.

claim: A simple implementation of spatial proofreading is via compartmentalization where substrates and effectors are localized in two spatially separated compartments.
source: A particularly simple implementation of our scheme is via compartmentalization – substrates and effectors are localized in two spatially separated compartments with the enzyme–substrate complex having to travel from one to another to complete the reaction.
evidence: This is proposed as a simple implementation scenario.

claim: In polarized, asymmetric cells, gene expression often needs to be spatially regulated.
source: For example, in polarized, asymmetric cells (e.g. budding yeast or neuronal cells) gene expression often needs to be spatially regulated (Parton et al., 2014; Martin and Ephrussi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parton et al., 2014 and Martin and Ephrussi, 2009.

claim: Spatial regulation of gene expression is achieved with designated ribonucleoproteins that bind specific mRNAs near the cell nucleus, perform a biased random walk to the mRNA localization site and deliver them for translation.
source: Such regulation is achieved with designated ribonucleoproteins that bind specific mRNAs near the cell nucleus, perform a biased random walk to the mRNA localization site and deliver them for translation.
evidence: This describes a known biological mechanism.

claim: During transport, mRNAs are protected from ribosome binding and when they unbind, they are subject to degradation which would prevent rebinding events at intermediate locations.
source: During transport, mRNAs are protected from ribosome binding and when they unbind, they are subject to degradation which would prevent rebinding events at intermediate locations.
evidence: This describes features of the mRNA localization mechanism.

claim: Non-vesicular transport of lipids between membrane-bound domains is mediated by lipid-transfer proteins.
source: Another example process is the non-vesicular transport of lipids between the membrane–bound domains of the cells (e.g. the ER, mitochondria, the Golgi apparatus, or the plasma membrane). This transport mechanism is mediated by lipid-transfer proteins that bind lipids on the donor membrane, diffuse to the acceptor membrane and upon interacting with it, undergo a conformational change, delivering the 'cargo' (Lev, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lev, 2010.

claim: Some lipid-transfer proteins are known to exhibit specificity for their cognate substrates.
source: given the fact that some of the lipid-transfer proteins are known to exhibit specificity for their cognate substrates.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about lipid-transfer proteins.

claim: Spatial proofreading may be applicable as a quality control mechanism in protein secretion pathways.
source: Our scheme may also be applicable as a quality control mechanism in protein secretion pathways (Ellgaard and Helenius, 2003; Arvan et al., 2002)
evidence: This is proposed as a potential application with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial proofreading may be applicable in high-fidelity targeting of membrane proteins mediated by signal recognition particles.
source: in high-fidelity targeting of membrane proteins mediated by signal recognition particles (Rao et al., 2016; Chio et al., 2017)
evidence: This is proposed as a potential application with supporting citations.

claim: Spatial proofreading may be applicable in selective glycosylation reactions in the Golgi apparatus.
source: as well as in selective glycosylation reactions in the Golgi apparatus (Jaiman and Thattai, 2020).
evidence: This is proposed as a potential application with supporting citation.

claim: Recent advances have been made in generating synthetic morphogen patterns in multicellular organisms.
source: Lastly, considering the recent advances in generating synthetic morphogen patterns in multicellular organisms (Toda et al., 2020; Stapornwongkul et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Toda et al., 2020 and Stapornwongkul et al., 2020.

claim: Spatial proofreading could be employed in pathways acting on engineered protein gradients.
source: spatial proofreading could also be employed in pathways acting on engineered protein gradients.
evidence: This is proposed as a potential application.

claim: Enzymatic reactions may acquire de novo proofreading capabilities by coupling to pre-existing spatial gradients in the cell.
source: This suggests that enzymatic reactions may acquire de novo proofreading capabilities by coupling to pre-existing spatial gradients in the cell.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the work.
